criteria.long_description: Names the chapter and the opening words, and two sentences say accurately what happens in the passage.

ratings.long_description: Names the chapter and the opening words, and two sentences say accurately what happens in the passage.
Location named, but the two sentences are vague or describe the wrong thing.
No set-up.

criteria.long_description: Reads the passage as written. Unfamiliar words and names are attempted and pronounced clearly.

ratings.long_description: Reads the passage as written. Unfamiliar words and names are attempted and pronounced clearly.
Frequent misreadings, or lines skipped.
Passage not read, or far under length.

criteria.long_description: Steady pace a listener can follow. Audible throughout. Phrasing and emphasis match what the sentence means.

ratings.long_description: Steady pace a listener can follow. Audible throughout. Phrasing and emphasis match what the sentence means.
Rushed, flat, or hard to hear in places.
Inaudible or unintelligible.

criteria.long_description: Completes the chosen response and points at something specific in the passage just read, not at the story in general.

ratings.long_description: Completes the chosen response and points at something specific in the passage just read, not at the story in general.
Starts the response but stays general, or answers only part of it.
No response after the reading.

rubrics.title: The Outsiders · Loyalty and the Divide (optional) Rubric

criteria.long_description: A clear claim about loyalty, the divide, or staying gold, backed by a specific novel event described in the student's own words, plus a substantive reply that engages a classmate's reasoning.

ratings.long_description: A clear claim about loyalty, the divide, or staying gold, backed by a specific novel event described in the student's own words, plus a substantive reply that engages a classmate's reasoning.
A claim or a reply is present but thin: no text detail, or a reply that only says "I agree" without adding anything.
Missing post, or off topic.

criteria.long_description: How well the work shows the student understands *The Outsiders* and the theme they chose to analyze.

ratings.long_description: Shows a clear, accurate grasp of the novel and the chosen theme (loyalty, family, or staying gold). The essay reflects what the book actually shows about that theme.
Understands the main events and the theme. A small detail may be off, but the central idea is sound.
Some understanding, but with gaps or a misread of the theme or the plot.
Little accurate understanding of the text or the theme.

criteria.long_description: How well the claim is supported with specific, well-chosen evidence from the student's own copy, and how well that evidence is explained.

ratings.long_description: A clear thesis is backed by two or three well-chosen events or details, cited in MLA format (author's name and chapter), and each is explained so the reasoning is easy to follow. A correct Works Cited entry for the novel is included.
A thesis with supporting evidence, cited in MLA format with only minor slips (a missing Works Cited entry or an inconsistent locator); explanations are present but may be thin in a spot.
A thesis with little evidence, evidence that is named but not explained, or citations missing the author's name or the chapter.
No clear thesis, no real evidence, or no attempt at citation.

criteria.long_description: How clear, organized, and carefully made the essay is.

ratings.long_description: Writing is well organized and easy to follow; sentences are clear. Few errors.
Mostly clear and organized; a few errors or rough spots that do not block understanding.
Hard to follow in places; errors get in the way.
Unclear or disorganized; the theme is hard to see.

criteria.long_description: The classical formation lever. Rewards naming the limits of one's own reasoning and using evidence fairly.

ratings.long_description: Uses evidence fairly, does not overstate, and names where the argument is strong and where it is less certain. The essay is honest about where its evidence is strong and where it is less certain.
Uses evidence fairly with no clear overreach; some honest awareness of the evidence's limits.
Stretches evidence to fit, or claims more than the work shows.
Evidence is misused or invented.

assignments.title: The Outsiders · The Trailer
assignments.html:
The Outsiders · The Trailer
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Recorded Production
25 pointsRecord / Upload Media2 attempts
The Trailer
 
A book trailer voiceover. The narrator sets up the story without giving away the ending, reads one passage as written, then makes the pitch.
›Format. Book trailer, voiceover.
›Voice. One narrator.
›Subject. The Outsiders.
›Total runtime. 3 to 5 minutes.
Run sheet
 
1
Cold open · :20 to :30
Say the book, the chapter, and the passage’s opening words, then two sentences on what happens in the passage.
2
The passage · 1:30 to 2:30
Read the passage aloud, as written.
3
The pitch · 1:00 to 2:00
Complete one angle from the three below.
4
Title card · :10
Title and author, once more. One sentence.
01 · Cold open
 

Opening line: “______, by ______. ______ (the situation in one line). This is from Chapter ___, the passage that begins ‘______.’” Other wording is permitted if it carries the same facts.

02 · The passage
 
›Source. The Outsiders, Chapters 1 to 10, from your own copy.
›Length. 350 to 550 words.
›Text. Read as written. No summarising, skipping, or paraphrase.
›Prep. Two rehearsals before recording.
›Names. Unfamiliar names are attempted aloud, not skipped.
›Strong passages. A moment where loyalty and survival pull apart, or where Ponyboy sees someone differently than before. No passage from the last two chapters of that reading (no spoilers in a trailer). Choose a passage without swearing or a fight’s injuries in it.
03 · The pitch
 

Complete one. Equal weight.

A · Why this moment
Talk it through. 1 to 2 min. Answer two. Each answer points at a line in the passage.
• What the passage shows about a character that was not clear before it.
• One word the author chose here, and what a different word would lose.
• What changed in the reading when it was said aloud instead of read silently.
• How the passage bears on the question: what divides the greasers and the Socs, and what stays the same on both sides?
B · The case
Make the case. 1 to 2 min. Argue one debatable point about the passage. Take the side most listeners will not.
• Name the arguable point: a choice, a line with two readings, or an author’s decision.
• State the position in one sentence.
• Quote the words that support it.
• State the strongest objection fairly, then answer it.
C · One moment recut
Change one thing. 1 to 2 min. Change one moment inside the passage.
• Name the exact sentence or moment.
• Describe the replacement in enough detail to picture it.
• State what the author’s version does that the replacement does not, and which works better.
04 · Title card
 

Title and author, once more, in one sentence. About ten seconds.

Delivery
 
›Recorder. Record / Upload Media records into Canvas.
›Alternate. Use a phone or any recorder, then upload the file.
›Track. Audio only is complete. Video is permitted, never required.
›Attempts. Two. The later attempt is graded.
›Continuity. One take, four segments, in order.
Done when
 
☐Segment 01 names the chapter and the passage’s opening words and says what happens in it.
☐The passage is read aloud, in full, as written.
☐One angle is completed after the reading.
☐The angle points at a specific line, not the story in general.
☐Audible the whole way through.

assignments.title: The Outsiders Final Project
assignments.html:
The Outsiders Final Project
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Final Project
40 pointsFile uploadTwo filesGraded with a rubric
The question
 
What does The Outsiders say about loyalty, family, or what it means to stay gold, and how does Hinton build that idea across the novel?

Answer it in a literary-analysis essay of about 500 to 700 words. Any of the three themes can earn full marks when it is backed by moments from the book.

Write your essay
 
1
Choose one theme and write your thesis.
Pick one theme: loyalty, family, or staying gold. Write one clear sentence that states what The Outsiders says about it. This is your thesis. Put it at the end of a short opening paragraph that sets up the question.
2
Give your evidence and explain it.
Use two or three specific moments from your own copy of the book. Cite each one in MLA format: Hinton’s last name plus the chapter, for example (Hinton, Ch. 8). If you already name Hinton in your sentence, just give the chapter. After each one, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your point. Do not just name the event; explain what it means for your claim.
3
Write a conclusion.
End with two or three sentences that restate your thesis in fresh words and say what Hinton seems to want readers to understand about the theme you chose.
4
Add your Works Cited entry.
At the end of your document, add one entry for the novel: Hinton, S. E. The Outsiders. Then the publisher and the year, both from your own copy.
5
Be honest about your reasoning.
If a detail only partly fits your claim, say so. If the novel seems to say two things at once about your theme, acknowledge that. Naming where your evidence is strong and where it is less certain makes your essay stronger, not weaker.
Upload two files
 
1
Your essay.
A Word file named LastName_OS_FinalEssay, or a PDF of it.
2
The PDF from the Write Your Essay lesson.
It shows your case file and the revision of your essay.

40 points, graded with the rubric below.

Success criteria
 
☐A clear thesis names one theme and states what the novel says about it.
☐Two or three moments from your own copy, each cited in MLA format (author plus chapter).
☐Each moment is explained, not just named or quoted.
☐A conclusion ties the essay back to the theme you chose.
☐A Works Cited entry for the novel appears at the end of the document.
☐The essay is honest about where its evidence is strong and where it is less certain.
☐Both files are submitted together.
Before you submit
 
☐Your essay is written in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐The file is named LastName_OS_FinalEssay (for example, Garcia_OS_FinalEssay).
☐Line spacing is double throughout. Your name, the course, and the date are at the upper left, with a real title, centered, above your writing.
☐The title is set as a heading, and the body font is readable (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐It is saved in your OneDrive, in Optima > ELA > your course folder, and you confirmed it is there.
Skill you are practicing: creating and formatting a Word document; using digital tools to produce and share writing.
Rubric
 
Understanding of the text (10 pts)
Excellent (10)Shows a clear, accurate grasp of the novel and the chosen theme (loyalty, family, or staying gold). The essay reflects what the book actually shows about that theme.
Proficient (7.5)Understands the main events and the theme. A small detail may be off, but the central idea is sound.
Developing (5)Some understanding, but with gaps or a misread of the theme or the plot.
Beginning (2.5)Little accurate understanding of the text or the theme.
Quality of reasoning and evidence (10 pts)
Excellent (10)A clear thesis is backed by two or three well-chosen events or details, cited in MLA format (author’s name and chapter), and each is explained so the reasoning is easy to follow. A correct Works Cited entry for the novel is included.
Proficient (7.5)A thesis with supporting evidence, cited in MLA format with only minor slips (a missing Works Cited entry or an inconsistent locator); explanations are present but may be thin in a spot.
Developing (5)A thesis with little evidence, evidence that is named but not explained, or citations missing the author’s name or the chapter.
Beginning (2.5)No clear thesis, no real evidence, or no attempt at citation.
Clarity and precision (10 pts)
Excellent (10)Writing is well organized and easy to follow; sentences are clear. Few errors.
Proficient (7.5)Mostly clear and organized; a few errors or rough spots that do not block understanding.
Developing (5)Hard to follow in places; errors get in the way.
Beginning (2.5)Unclear or disorganized; the theme is hard to see.
Intellectual honesty (10 pts)
Excellent (10)Uses evidence fairly, does not overstate, and names where the argument is strong and where it is less certain. The essay is honest about where its evidence is strong and where it is less certain.
Proficient (7.5)Uses evidence fairly with no clear overreach; some honest awareness of the evidence’s limits.
Developing (5)Stretches evidence to fit, or claims more than the work shows.
Beginning (2.5)Evidence is misused or invented.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 1 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Week 1
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 1 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 1 Quiz

questions.text: The Outsiders is told in the first person by Ponyboy. What does that mean for the reader?

answers.text: We can see inside every character's mind.
We know only what Ponyboy sees, thinks, and chooses to tell us.
The author steps in between chapters to explain events.
Several characters take turns telling the story.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy says "I." We get his eyes and his feelings, and nothing he cannot see.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who says "I" in this book? Can that person see inside Darry's head, or a Soc's?

questions.text: Ponyboy explains the word "Soc" in Chapter 1. What does he say it is short for?

answers.text: Social workers who visit families on the East Side.
A private club for students at Ponyboy's school.
The Socials, "the West-side rich kids" (Hinton, Ch. 1).
Southern Oklahoma Cars, a club for car lovers.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Ponyboy says Soc is the abbreviation for the Socials, the rich kids from the West Side.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find where Ponyboy says he isn't sure how to spell it. What does he say it stands for?

questions.text: Lying in bed, Ponyboy says Soda "looked like some Greek god come to earth" (Hinton, Ch. 1). What kind of figurative language is this?

answers.text: Simile
Metaphor
Personification
Alliteration

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The comparison uses like, so it is a simile.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the signal word. Does the comparison use like or as?

questions.text: Cherry says Dally "looked as hard as nails and twice as tough" (Hinton, Ch. 2). What does this comparison suggest about how she sees him?

answers.text: She thinks he must work long, hard hours with his hands.
She thinks he is sick and tired of the drive-in.
She thinks he is joking with her.
She sees him as dangerous and impossible to soften.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Nails are hard and sharp. Cherry sees Dally as someone nothing gets through to.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What is a nail like? What would a person "as hard as nails" be like to deal with?

questions.text: At the drive-in, Cherry refuses to drink the Coke Dally brought her, but Marcia finishes hers. What can a reader infer?

answers.text: Marcia likes Dally much more than Cherry ever could.
Cherry acts on principle, while Marcia is more easygoing.
Cherry is not thirsty.
Marcia is too afraid of Dally to say no to anything.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy notices the two girls are not alike: Cherry meant what she said, and Marcia saw no reason to waste a free Coke.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An inference goes beyond what is stated. What does each girl's choice show about the kind of person she is?

questions.text: After the Socs run off, Darry tells Ponyboy, "You don't ever think" (Hinton, Ch. 1). Why is Darry upset?

answers.text: Ponyboy lost the only jacket he owned on the way home.
Ponyboy started the fight with the Socs.
Ponyboy walked home alone without using his head.
Ponyboy was late for dinner and Darry had waited.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Darry is angry that Ponyboy walked home by himself, though he could have asked for a ride.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What was Ponyboy doing when the Socs found him? Why would Darry call that not thinking?

questions.text: Why is Keith Mathews called Two-Bit?

answers.text: He once sold an old car to Steve for a single quarter.
He is the second-oldest boy in Ponyboy's gang.
He spends exactly two bits on every movie he sees.
"he always had to get his two-bits worth in" (Hinton, Ch. 1).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two-Bit can't stop making remarks, so he always adds his "two-bits worth."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the start of Two-Bit's portrait in Chapter 1. What can't he stop doing?

questions.text: Cherry tells Ponyboy, "That's like saying all you greasers are like Dallas Winston" (Hinton, Ch. 2). What is her point?

answers.text: Judging a whole group by its worst members is unfair.
Dally is the leader of every greaser in town.
Greasers should try to be more like Dally.
She wants Ponyboy to stop being a greaser.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Cherry says not every Soc is cruel, just as not every greaser is like Dally.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Cherry is answering what Ponyboy said about the Socs. What is she asking him not to do?

questions.text:
What tense is the verb works?

Example sentence: Soda works full time at the gas station.

answers.text: past
future
past perfect
present

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Works tells what Soda does now, as a regular thing, so it is present tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is this happening now or always, already done, or still to come?

questions.text: Which sentence uses the past tense?

answers.text: Example sentence: Ponyboy will remember every detail of the movie.
Example sentence: Ponyboy remembered every detail of the movie.
Example sentence: Ponyboy remembers every detail of the movie.
Example sentence: Ponyboy is remembering every detail of the movie.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Remembered shows something already done.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the verb that shows the action is finished.

questions.text:
What is the verb phrase had started?

Example sentence: By the time Two-Bit arrived, the movie had already started.

answers.text: future tense
present tense
past perfect
future perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Had plus a past verb marks the earlier of two past moments: the movie started before Two-Bit arrived.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When had comes before a past verb, it points to the earlier of two past events. What is that form called?

questions.text: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: Cherry turned around; she told Dally to leave.
Example sentence: Cherry turned around; because Dally was rude.
Example sentence: Cherry wanted; Dally to leave.
Example sentence: Cherry had one friend with her; Marcia.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both sides are complete thoughts, so a semicolon can join them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon needs a complete thought on both sides. Cover each side. Can it stand alone?

questions.text: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: Two-Bit named: the gang's two rules.
Example sentence: Two-Bit named the gang's two rules: stick together, and don't get caught.
Example sentence: Two-Bit: named the gang's two rules.
Example sentence: Two-Bit named the gang's two rules, stick: together.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A complete thought comes first, and the colon opens the list.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon comes after a complete thought and opens a list or an explanation. Which option does that?

questions.text:
What does the colon do in this sentence?

Example sentence: Darry had one worry about Ponyboy: he never used his head.

answers.text: It joins two lists.
It replaces a question mark.
It introduces the explanation of Darry's worry.
It shows a list of verbs is coming.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The words after the colon explain what the worry was.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read what comes after the colon. What does it tell you about the words before it?

questions.text:
What does the pair of dashes do in this sentence?

Example sentence: Steve—Soda's best friend—could fix almost any car.

answers.text: It sets off an extra comment that could be taken out.
It joins two complete thoughts into one sentence.
It introduces a list.
It shows that someone is speaking.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Cover the words between the dashes. The sentence still works: they are an aside.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the sentence without the words between the dashes. Does it still make sense? What are those words doing?

questions.text:
Which mark belongs in the blank?

Example sentence: Ponyboy needed three things that night __ a ride, some company, and a little luck.

answers.text: a semicolon (;)
a comma (,)
a period (.)
a colon (:)

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A complete thought comes first, and a list follows, so a colon belongs there.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What comes after the blank: a complete thought, or a list? Which mark opens a list?

quizzes.title: Week 2 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 2 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Week 2
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 2 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 2 Quiz

questions.text: In Chapter 3, Cherry says the Socs and the greasers are divided by more than money. How does she describe the difference?

answers.text: Greasers are better at sports.
Greasers feel things strongly, and Socs hide their feelings.
Socs and greasers go to different schools.
Socs work harder in school than greasers do, so they get ahead.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Cherry says the greasers are the more emotional ones, and the Socs keep their feelings cool and hidden.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Cherry is talking about what each side feels and shows, not about sports or school. What does she say each side does with its feelings?

questions.text: When Ponyboy finally reaches the country, why isn't he as happy as he expected to be?

answers.text: It is colder than the city.
The farmer is unkind to him.
Johnny wants to turn around and go straight back home.
He may never see his brothers or friends again.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. He had pictured the country as an escape, and now he sees what he has left behind.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 4. What does Ponyboy realize he has lost by leaving town?

questions.text: Ponyboy ends Chapter 3 by telling the reader that he was wrong to think things could not get worse. What is this an example of?

answers.text: Foreshadowing
Flashback
Simile
Personification

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The older Ponyboy hints that something bad is coming before it happens. That is foreshadowing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is the writer going back in time, comparing two things, or hinting at what comes next?

questions.text: Which of these is an analytical claim?

answers.text: In Chapter 3, Ponyboy tells Cherry about Mickey Mouse, the horse Soda loved and lost.
After the movie, Johnny and Ponyboy lie on their backs in the vacant lot and fall asleep.
Ponyboy's outburst at Johnny shows his anger at Darry spilling onto a friend.
Ponyboy is fourteen and lives with his two older brothers.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A claim says what something means, and a reader could argue with it. The others only tell what happens or who someone is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Three of these only report facts. Which one says what a moment means?

questions.text: How does Chapter 3 prepare the reader for what happens in the park in Chapter 4?

answers.text: It shows the Socs and greasers becoming friends.
It explains the rules of a rumble.
It tells the reader exactly what will happen, so there is no surprise.
It keeps raising the tension before anything breaks.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The chapter piles up worries and warnings, so the reader feels trouble coming.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how the chapter feels as it goes on. Does it calm down, or does the pressure keep building?

questions.text: Why does Darry shout at Ponyboy when he gets home?

answers.text: Ponyboy had been fighting with Socs.
He was out until two, and Darry was scared.
Ponyboy had lost Soda's sweat shirt.
Soda told Darry that Ponyboy was out with Cherry Valance.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Darry's anger comes from fear. Ponyboy had been out far too late.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at how late it is when Ponyboy walks in. What would Darry have been feeling while he waited?

questions.text: Cherry says she could fall in love with Dallas Winston and hopes she never sees him again. What does she mean?

answers.text: She has already forgotten Dally.
She plans to meet Dally at school.
Part of her is drawn to Dally, though he is trouble.
She wants Ponyboy to carry a message to Dally for her.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. She feels the pull of someone exciting and dangerous, and she knows it would not be good for her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: She says two things that seem to disagree. What would make a person say both?

questions.text: Ponyboy lies easily to the farmer. What does Soda say that easy lying comes from?

answers.text: Reading so much
Growing up with Two-Bit
Watching too many movies
Being the youngest

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Ponyboy says Soda blames it on all his reading.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the lie Ponyboy tells the farmer. What does Ponyboy say right after, about where Soda thinks it comes from?

questions.text:
Which word is the subject noun?

Example sentence: The sunburned farmer stopped his tractor on the road.

answers.text: sunburned
stopped
farmer
road

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Farmer is the noun the sentence is about, the one that did the stopping.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The subject is the noun that does the action. Who stopped?

questions.text:
Which word is the adverb?

Example sentence: Cherry looked at Ponyboy gently.

answers.text: gently
looked
Cherry
Ponyboy

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Gently tells how Cherry looked, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adverb tells how, when, or where something happens. Which word tells how she looked?

questions.text: The words a, an, and the belong to which group?

answers.text: pronouns that point to nouns
prepositions that show place
interjections that stand apart
article adjectives

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A, an, and the are article adjectives. They come before a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: These three small words always sit in front of a noun. Which group do they belong to?

questions.text:
Which word is a conjunction?

Example sentence: Johnny and Ponyboy ran for several blocks.

answers.text: for
and
several
ran

questions.feedback_correct: Right. And joins the two names, so it is a conjunction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A conjunction joins words or groups of words. Which word joins Johnny and Ponyboy?

questions.text: You want to put the spotlight on what happened, not on who did it. Which voice is usually the better choice?

answers.text: Passive voice
Active voice
Both work the same in every sentence.
Neither; use a question instead.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Passive voice puts the action first and can leave the doer out.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In which voice does the doer come first? Which one lets you leave the doer out?

questions.text: Which sentence is in active voice?

answers.text: Example sentence: The porch light was left on.
Example sentence: The freight was boarded in the dark by the boys.
Example sentence: Two-Bit tore up Marcia's phone number.
Example sentence: Soda's horse was taken away one day.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two-Bit is the doer, and he comes first. He did the tearing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In active voice the doer comes first and does the action. In the others, the action happens to something. Which sentence starts with the doer?

questions.text: In a passive-voice sentence, the verb usually includes...

answers.text: an action verb with no helping verb
a helping verb and a past participle
two action verbs in a row
an article adjective right before the verb

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A helping verb such as was plus a past participle, as in was taken, builds the passive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think of was taken or was left. What two parts make up that verb?

questions.text:
Which is the correct active-voice rewrite?

Example sentence: Ponyboy was startled by Cherry's question.

answers.text: Ponyboy startled Cherry's question.
Ponyboy had been startled.
Cherry's question was startling Ponyboy.
Cherry's question startled Ponyboy.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The question did the startling, so it comes first, and Ponyboy receives it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In the original, who or what did the startling? Put that first and make the verb active.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 3 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Week 3
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 3 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 3 Quiz

questions.text: Where do Ponyboy and Johnny hide in Chapters 5 and 6?

answers.text: A barn at the edge of town
An old church on top of a hill
Dally's apartment
A friend's basement on the other side of town

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dally sends them to an abandoned church on Jay Mountain.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dally sends them out of town by freight train. Picture the building at the top of the hill.

questions.text: In Frost's poem, gold is the color of the first new leaves. What does gold most likely stand for when Ponyboy recites it?

answers.text: Money, and what greasers don't have
Loyalty between friends
What is fresh and good, and doesn't last
Only the color of that one sunrise, nothing more

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Gold is the first, best part of a thing, and the poem says how quickly it goes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask what the poem says happens to gold. Why would a sunrise make Ponyboy think of a poem about losing things?

questions.text: Ponyboy says he could not tell most of the gang about the sunrise and the poem. Whom does he say would understand?

answers.text: Johnny, Soda, and maybe Cherry
Darry and Two-Bit
Dally, because Dally is the most real of them
Only Johnny, nobody else

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy names Johnny and Soda, and then adds Cherry Valance.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find where Ponyboy lists the people who just do not get it. Then find the people who do. He names more than one.

questions.text: Which of these is a theme statement?

answers.text: Friendship
In Chapter 5, Ponyboy and Johnny spend about five days hiding in the old church on the hill.
The setting of the church chapters
Friends can help each other see what they would miss.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A theme statement is a full sentence that says something about life, not just what happens in the story.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A topic is one word or a phrase. A plot fact tells what happens. Which option makes a claim about people?

questions.text: Why do the police think the boys went to Texas?

answers.text: Johnny left a note saying so.
Dally let it slip at the station.
Someone saw them on a bus going south.
Two-Bit went to Texas to look for them.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dally says he let it slip at the station that they were headed for Texas, so that is where the police are looking.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who got hauled in to the station and had the chance to say something? Did anyone actually see the boys leave?

questions.text: How does Ponyboy guess the church caught fire?

answers.text: He and Johnny may have dropped a lit cigarette.
The picnic grill was left burning.
Lightning hit the old roof the night before the picnic.
The Socs set it to find the boys.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy thinks the fire may have started with a cigarette he and Johnny dropped, and he is afraid it was their fault.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read what Ponyboy says to Johnny at the top of the hill. What does he blame?

questions.text: What does Dally do when Johnny is still inside the church?

answers.text: He drives off to get help in town.
He shouts for the firemen to hurry.
He goes back in to get him out.
He waits by the car the whole time.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dally goes back into the church for Johnny.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dally does not wait. Read what he does when he sees Johnny has not come out.

questions.text: Johnny says the Southern gentlemen in Gone with the Wind remind him of Dally. Naming another book like this is an example of...

answers.text: a flashback
a simile
foreshadowing
an allusion

questions.feedback_correct: Right. An allusion is a reference to another work the reader may know.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A flashback goes back in this story's own time, and foreshadowing hints at what comes later in it. What do we call a reference to a different book?

questions.text:
Which part is a prepositional phrase?

Example sentence: Ponyboy ducked inside the old church door.

answers.text: Ponyboy ducked inside the old church
old church
inside the old church door
ducked inside

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The phrase starts with the preposition inside and ends with the noun door.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition and ends with a noun. Which word starts it?

questions.text:
What type of sentence is this?

Example sentence: The whistle sounded, and Ponyboy answered it.

answers.text: Compound
Simple
Complex
A fragment

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two complete thoughts are joined by and, so the sentence is compound.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the complete thoughts. Can each side of the comma stand alone?

questions.text:
What type of sentence is this?

Example sentence: Because the mornings were cold, the boys slept huddled together.

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Fragment
Complex

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Because the mornings were cold cannot stand alone, and it is attached to a complete thought. That makes the sentence complex.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Does the first part stand alone? Which kind of sentence has one part that cannot?

questions.text:
What part of speech is carefully?

Example sentence: Johnny listened carefully while Ponyboy explained the book.

answers.text: Adjective, because it describes Johnny
Adverb, because it tells how he listened
Preposition, because it comes after the verb
Noun, because it names something Johnny did

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Carefully tells how Johnny listened, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adverb tells how, when, or where. Which word tells how he listened?

questions.text: A student wrote: When Dally finally came. Can this stand alone as a sentence?

answers.text: Yes, because it has a subject and a verb
Yes, if it ends with a period
No, because it has no subject
No, because it is a dependent clause

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When turns the group into a dependent clause, so it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: It has a subject and a verb, but does the thought feel finished? Read it and ask what happened when Dally came.

questions.text:
Which part is the dependent clause?

Example sentence: Although Ponyboy loved his long hair, he let Johnny cut it.

answers.text: he let Johnny cut it
Ponyboy loved his long hair, and he let Johnny cut it
Although Ponyboy loved his long hair
let Johnny cut

questions.feedback_correct: Right. It has a subject and a verb, but Although keeps it from standing alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which part starts with a word like although and cannot stand alone as a sentence?

questions.text:
Which word is an adjective describing mirror?

Example sentence: Ponyboy looked into the old cracked mirror.

answers.text: cracked
looked into
into
Ponyboy

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Cracked describes the mirror. It tells what kind.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adjective describes a noun. Which word tells what kind of mirror it is?

questions.text:
What type of sentence is this?

Example sentence: Dally grinned and handed Ponyboy a letter.

answers.text: Compound, because it has and
Simple
Complex
Fragment

questions.feedback_correct: Right. One subject does two things, grinned and handed. That is a compound verb, so the sentence is simple.
questions.feedback_incorrect: And joins two verbs here, not two sentences. Is there a second subject?

quizzes.title: Week 4 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 4 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Week 4
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 4 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 4 Quiz

questions.text:
Which word needs a capital letter?

Example sentence: Ponyboy and johnny hid out near a small town.

answers.text: small town
hid out
johnny
near a

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Johnny is the name of one particular person, so it starts with a capital.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the name of one particular person.

questions.text: Which sentence capitalizes the title before a name correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: Mrs. Mathews let Two-Bit get away with almost anything.
Example sentence: mrs. Mathews let Two-Bit get away with almost anything at all.
Example sentence: Mrs. mathews let Two-Bit get away with almost anything at all.
Example sentence: MRS. MATHEWS let Two-Bit get away with almost anything.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A title before a name, like Mrs., is capitalized along with the name.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A title used with a name, and the name itself, both start with a capital. Which sentence does that without extra capitals?

questions.text:
Which end mark belongs at the end of this sentence?

Example sentence: Did Two-Bit bring the book for Johnny

answers.text: a period
a comma
an exclamation point
a question mark

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The sentence asks something, so it ends with a question mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is the sentence telling, asking, or shouting? Which mark goes with a question?

questions.text:
Which words should NOT be capitalized?

Example sentence: Soda and Steve work at the Gas Station.

answers.text: Soda and Steve
Gas Station
Soda
Steve

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A gas station is a common noun, not the name of one particular place, so it is not capitalized here.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A capital goes with the name of a particular person, place, or brand. Which words only name a kind of place?

questions.text:
Which choice writes the book's title correctly?

Example sentence: Before this book, the class read The Call of the Wild.

answers.text: "The Call of the Wild" in quotation marks
THE CALL OF THE WILD in capitals
The Call of the Wild in italics
the call of the wild in lowercase letters

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The title of a whole book goes in italics, or is underlined when handwritten.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A book is a long work. Which mark of style do long works get? Short works get quotation marks.

questions.text:
Which choice writes the poem's title correctly?

Example sentence: Dickinson's poem Hope Is the Thing with Feathers is printed in a book of stories.

answers.text: "Hope Is the Thing with Feathers" in quotation marks
Hope Is the Thing with Feathers in italics, the way a book title is written
HOPE IS THE THING WITH FEATHERS in capitals
Hope Is the Thing with Feathers with no marks, underlined twice

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A poem is a short work, so its title goes in quotation marks, even in a book of stories.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A poem is a short piece of writing. Which mark goes around the titles of short works?

questions.text: Which sentence introduces the quotation correctly?

answers.text: Ponyboy tells Cherry quietly "You can see it good from the East Side, too" (Hinton, Ch. 8).
Ponyboy tells Cherry; "You can see it good from the East Side, too" (Hinton, Ch. 8).
Ponyboy tells Cherry. "You can see it good from the East Side, too" (Hinton, Ch. 8).
Ponyboy tells Cherry, "You can see it good from the East Side, too" (Hinton, Ch. 8).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A comma sets off the words that introduce a quotation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A short introduction like Ponyboy tells Cherry needs one mark before the opening quotation mark. Which mark?

questions.text: Which version places the period and the citation correctly?

answers.text: "Socs were just guys after all." (Hinton, Ch. 7)
"Socs were just guys after all" (Hinton, Ch. 7).
"Socs were just guys after all." (Hinton, Ch. 7).
"Socs were just guys after all" (Ch. 7, Hinton).

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When a citation follows a quotation, the closing quotation mark comes first, then the citation, then the period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Where does the sentence end when the citation is part of it? Check the author's name and chapter order too.

questions.text: As Chapter 8 goes on, what does Ponyboy feel about the night ahead?

answers.text: Excited, because the greasers are sure to win the rumble
Calm, because the doctors say Johnny is getting better
Afraid that something will happen that no one can stop
Bored, because the reporters have finally gone home

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy cannot shake the feeling that something is coming that no one can prevent.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read how Ponyboy talks about the night ahead. Is he eager, calm, or uneasy?

questions.text: Which moment shows loyalty as simply being there for someone?

answers.text: Two-Bit refuses to leave until he sees Johnny.
Dally argues with a nurse because he wants to leave.
Steve tells Ponyboy not to worry about a boys' home.
Two-Bit makes jokes about Ponyboy's short haircut.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two-Bit stays until he has seen Johnny for himself.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Loyalty here means showing up and staying. Which character stays put for a friend?

questions.text: Which idea do Chapters 7 and 8 keep showing through what the characters do?

answers.text: Randy Adderson drives a blue Mustang to the Tasty Freeze.
Ponyboy fixes breakfast for his two brothers one morning.
The newspaper prints a picture of the three brothers.
People on both sides of a line can feel the same pain.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Randy, Cherry, and the greasers all show feelings that cross the line between them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An idea is something a reader takes away, not just a thing that happens. Which option says what the chapters seem to mean?

questions.text: Randy says, "You can't win, even if you whip us" (Hinton, Ch. 7). What does he mean?

answers.text: The Socs have more fighters, so the greasers will lose.
Fighting won't change who is on top.
The police will stop the rumble before it starts.
Randy will tell the Socs to stay home that night.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Even a win would not change the gap between the two sides.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Randy says "even if you whip us." What does he think a win would still not fix?

questions.text: Ponyboy answers Randy, "you hate the whole world" (Hinton, Ch. 7). What is his point?

answers.text: Randy's bitterness comes from Randy.
The whole world really does hate the Socs for their money.
Ponyboy hates Randy for what the Socs did at the park.
Randy should leave town and start over somewhere else.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy says the hate is in Randy, not in the world around him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Randy blames money for everything. What does Ponyboy say about where the hate comes from?

questions.text: Why does Darry call Soda Pepsi-Cola that morning?

answers.text: He is teasing Soda for drinking so much soda pop.
It is Soda's real name, written on his birth papers.
He knows Soda is unhappy about Sandy.
He is angry that Soda overslept and is late for work.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Darry rarely uses the nickname. He uses it because he can tell Soda is hurting.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ponyboy explains why Darry uses a gentler name that day. What does Darry know about Soda?

questions.text: What does Ponyboy ask Two-Bit to keep from Darry?

answers.text: That he talked with Randy at the Tasty Freeze
That he met Cherry at the vacant lot that day
That he skipped the dishes and went to the movies
That he feels sick and feverish

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy does not want Darry to worry about how sick he feels.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what Ponyboy is trying to hide so that Darry does not worry.

questions.text: When Ponyboy asks Cherry whether she can see the sunset from the West Side, what is he telling her?

answers.text: That he wants a ride in her red Corvette before dark
That the two sides share more than they think
That the East Side has the better view of the sky
That he forgives the Socs for everything at the park

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A sunset is something both sides can look at, so it shows what they share.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What does one sunset over both sides of town have to do with what divides them?

quizzes.title: Week 5 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 5 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Week 5
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 5 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 5 Quiz

questions.text: Both sides agree ahead of time to a planned fight with set rules. What does the novel call it?

answers.text: a showdown
a rumble
a riot
a standoff between gangs

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A rumble is set for a time and a place, with rules both sides accept.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the first lines of Chapter 9. What word does Ponyboy use for the planned fight?

questions.text: After the rumble, Dally takes Ponyboy to the hospital. Whom are they going to see?

answers.text: Two-Bit, who was hurt in the fight
Steve, who has broken ribs
Johnny
Cherry and Randy

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dally says Johnny wants to see Ponyboy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dally left the hospital himself to fight. Who is still there?

questions.text: At the rumble, Ponyboy notices that the Socs look like they could be going to the movies. What point is he making?

answers.text: People judge by looks, and the Socs look decent.
The Socs did not take the rumble seriously at all.
The Socs were planning to leave for a movie after it.
The greasers were dressed better than the Socs that night.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy says people usually go by looks, and the Socs look like ordinary kids.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read what he says right after. Why do people blame the greasers?

questions.text: Johnny hears that the greasers won the rumble and says fighting is useless. What does that show about him?

answers.text: Johnny wishes he had been at the rumble.
Johnny is angry that Dally fought without him.
Johnny thinks the Socs will want a second rumble very soon.
Johnny no longer believes fighting settles anything.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The win means nothing to him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Does Johnny smile at the news? Read his answer.

questions.text: At the start of Chapter 10, how does Ponyboy act as he walks away from the hospital?

answers.text: He goes straight to the police station.
He tells himself it didn't happen.
He runs to tell Cherry and Randy.
He goes looking for Dally to fight the Socs again.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He wanders for hours and will not believe it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the first page of Chapter 10. What does he keep telling himself?

questions.text: Which best describes a story's climax?

answers.text: The opening, where we meet the characters
The background history a reader needs to understand the story
The ending, where loose ends are tied up
The peak, where the main conflict is decided

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After the climax, nothing goes back to the way it was.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The climax is not the start or the end. Where is the tension at its highest?

questions.text: Which action in Chapter 10 best shows the brothers as a family?

answers.text: Two-Bit reads the newspaper in the living room.
Steve runs to the vacant lot with the others.
Darry sleeps in a chair by Ponyboy's bed.
A stranger gives Ponyboy a ride home.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Darry stays with Ponyboy while he is sick.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which action shows one brother taking care of another?

questions.text: In an argument, what does a counterclaim do?

answers.text: It states the other side fairly, so you can answer it.
It repeats your own claim in different words for emphasis.
It lists every event in the order it happened.
It gives up your claim when someone disagrees.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Then you show why your claim still holds.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A counterclaim does not give up. What does it name?

questions.text:
Which version places the comma correctly?

Example sentence: "I left my lunch on the counter" said Ms. Reyes.

answers.text: "I left my lunch on the counter," said, Ms. Reyes.
"I left my lunch on the counter", said Ms. Reyes.
"I left my lunch on the counter," said Ms. Reyes.
,"I left my lunch on the counter" said Ms. Reyes.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, before the speaker tag.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma sits at the end of the spoken words, tucked inside the mark. Which version puts it there and nowhere else?

questions.text:
Which is true?

Example sentence: Elena shouted, "Watch out for the step."

answers.text: It is correct as written.
The period belongs outside the mark.
The comma belongs after the opening mark.
It needs no quotation marks because of the tag.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The comma follows the tag, the spoken words are in marks, and the period goes inside.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each mark: a comma after the tag, marks around the words, and the period inside. Does anything need changing?

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: "Can we leave early?" Jordan, asked.
Example sentence: "Can we leave early," Jordan asked?
Example sentence: "Can we leave early." Jordan asked.
Example sentence: "Can we leave early?" Jordan asked.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The spoken words are a question, so the question mark goes inside the marks, and the sentence ends with a period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which mark belongs with a question, and where does the sentence about Jordan end?

questions.text:
What is the error?

Example sentence: Jordan replied, "The practice starts at four o'clock".

answers.text: The comma after replied should not be there.
The period should be inside the mark.
The words need no quotation marks.
Replied should start with a capital.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The final period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the end of the sentence. On which side of the closing mark does the period sit?

questions.text:
Why does The start with a capital letter?

Example sentence: "Keep the door closed," she reminded us. "The cat will escape."

answers.text: It begins a new sentence the speaker says.
Words after a speaker tag always start with a capital.
The speaker is talking louder now.
The cat is a name, so it needs a capital.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The tag ends one sentence, and the speaker starts a new one, so the new one begins with a capital.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the period before the quotation. Is the quotation the rest of the same sentence, or a fresh one?

questions.text:
Which version fixes it?

Example sentence: "I already told you the answer." he said with a shrug.

answers.text: "I already told you the answer." He said, with a shrug.
"I already told you the answer," he said with a shrug.
I already told you the answer, he said with a shrug.
"I already told you the answer" he said, with a shrug.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A comma replaces the period, and the tag stays lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The tag is not a new sentence. Which version ends the spoken part with a comma inside the marks?

questions.text:
What is missing?

Example sentence: Mr. Hale called from the hallway, Good morning everyone.

answers.text: A comma after morning, before everyone
A period at the very end of the sentence
A capital letter at the start of good
Quotation marks around the spoken words

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The words Mr. Hale says aloud need quotation marks.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which words did someone actually say aloud? What marks go around spoken words?

questions.text:
Which version is correct?

Example sentence: "The field is wet" said the coach "so practice is inside."

answers.text: "The field is wet," said the coach "so practice is inside."
"The field is wet," said the coach, "so practice is inside."
"The field is wet.", said the coach, "So practice is inside."
"The field is wet" said the coach, "so practice is inside".

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The tag is set off by commas on both sides, and the speaker's sentence continues in lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The tag interrupts one sentence. Which version puts a comma on each side of the tag?

quizzes.title: Week 6 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 6 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Week 6
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 6 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 6 Quiz

questions.text: In Chapter 11, who comes to the Curtis house to see Ponyboy before the hearing?

answers.text: Cherry Valance
Tim Shepard
Randy
Two-Bit

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Randy comes to check on Ponyboy before they see the judge.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the first visitor Darry announces.

questions.text:
Which word fits?

Example sentence: The cold weather began to ___ his recovery.

answers.text: effect
affect
effected
affection

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Affect is the verb, the action: began to affect.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Effect names a result. After began to, you need an action word.

questions.text: What is a frame narrative?

answers.text: A story set inside the story of its telling
A story told in a series of diary entries or letters
A story told by several narrators, one after another
A story whose ending is left open for the reader

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The frame is someone telling or writing the story, and the story sits inside it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think of the outside of a picture frame. Who is telling the story, and when?

questions.text: Which sentence uses the right word?

answers.text: Example sentence: Their going to the store after school.
Example sentence: There going to the store after school.
Example sentence: Their going to they're store after school.
Example sentence: They're going to the store after school.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. They're means they are. Say it the long way and it fits.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Say it the long way. Does they are fit in that spot?

questions.text: At the end of Chapter 12, what does Ponyboy decide to do?

answers.text: Ask the judge to let him live with Two-Bit
Write his English theme about what happened
Drop out and work at the gas station with Soda
Leave the gang and make friends with the Socs

questions.feedback_correct: Right. He decides to write it all down, starting with his English theme.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the last page. What does Ponyboy pick up?

questions.text: Which sentence uses its and it's correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: The gang had it's own rules, and its easy to see why.
Example sentence: The gang had its own rules, and its easy to see why.
Example sentence: The gang had it's own rules, and it's easy to see why.
Example sentence: The gang had its own rules, and it's easy to see why.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Its shows that something belongs to it, and it's means it is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try it is in each spot. Where does it fit?

questions.text: Why does the judge ask Ponyboy only about home and school?

answers.text: The doctor had talked with the judge first.
Darry had asked the judge to go easy on Ponyboy.
The Socs had already told the judge everything.
Ponyboy refused to answer questions about that night.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The doctor spoke with the judge before the hearing, and Ponyboy later learned why.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who had a long talk with the judge before the hearing began?

questions.text: Which sentence uses then and than correctly?

answers.text: Example sentence: He worked longer then anyone else, than took a break.
Example sentence: He worked longer then anyone else, then took a break.
Example sentence: He worked longer than anyone else, then took a break.
Example sentence: He worked longer than anyone else, than he took a break.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Than compares (longer than), and then tells when (then took a break).
questions.feedback_incorrect: One word compares and one tells time. Which is which?

questions.text: Soda says "it's like I'm the middleman in a tug o' war" (Hinton, Ch. 12). What does he mean?

answers.text: He likes being the one in the middle of the family.
His brothers' fights pull him two ways at once.
He wants Darry and Ponyboy to choose who is right.
He is tired of being the gang's peacemaker in fights.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He loves both brothers, so their fights pull him apart.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who is pulling, and who is stuck in the middle?

questions.text:
What is wrong?

Example sentence: The hearing had a big affect on the whole family.

answers.text: Hearing should be hearings, because a family is many people.
Whole should be hole, a word that sounds the same.
Affect should be effect, the noun for a result.
Nothing is wrong; affect names a result here.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A big effect is a result, and effect is the noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Does that word name an action or a result? This one names a result.

questions.text: In his note, how does Johnny feel about going back into the church for the children?

answers.text: He wishes he had waited for help.
He is angry that nobody thanked him.
He is proud the papers called him a hero.
It was worth it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. He writes that saving them was worth it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the note in your own copy. What does he say about the children?

questions.text: Which sentence has NO error?

answers.text: Example sentence: The gang kept its rules no matter what.
Example sentence: Their are three reasons for his choice.
Example sentence: The decision effected everyone in the gang differently.
Example sentence: He was taller then his older brother by an inch.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Its shows that the rules belong to the gang, so there is nothing to fix.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each sound-alike. Which sentence passes every check?

questions.text: In the park, what does Ponyboy suddenly realize about Darry?

answers.text: Darry blames Soda for all of their fights.
Darry is only twenty and can be scared too.
Darry is planning to quit roofing for a better job.
Darry has wanted to send him to a home all along.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Darry is only twenty, and he is as scared and lost as the rest of them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read what Ponyboy sees in Darry's face in the park.

questions.text:
Which proofreading pass would catch the error?

Example sentence: The brothers kept there promise.

answers.text: the spelling pass, letter by letter
the sentence-edge pass
the read-aloud pass, start to finish
the sound-alike pass

questions.feedback_correct: Right. There for their is a sound-alike mix-up.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is the word misspelled, or is it the wrong word that sounds the same?

questions.text: At the hearing, what do Darry and Soda answer when the judge asks if Dally was a good buddy of theirs?

answers.text: Darry says no, and Soda says yes.
They refuse to answer the judge.
They both say yes.
They say they barely knew him.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. They both say yes. They would not desert him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ponyboy says he was proud of both of them. Why?

questions.text:
What is wrong?

Example sentence: Him and Soda raced home from the park.

answers.text: Him should be He, because it is part of the subject.
Raced should be race, because the story happens now.
Park should have a capital, because it is a place.
Nothing is wrong; him is fine at the start of a sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Ask who raced. He and Soda did. Him cannot do the racing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask who raced home. Could him be the one doing the racing?

discussions.title: The Outsiders · Loyalty and the Divide (optional)
discussions.html:
The Outsiders · Loyalty and the Divide (optional)
7th Grade ELA · The Outsiders · Optional Discussion
10 pointsOptionalPost, then reply
Loyalty, the divide, and staying gold in The Outsiders.

The novel asks whether the things that divide the greasers and the Socs are as solid as they first appear, and whether what holds people together can reach across those lines.

Your post (one short paragraph, five to seven sentences)

State one claim about what The Outsiders says about loyalty, the greaser-Soc divide, or what it means to stay gold. Explain why you believe it, using one specific event from the novel described in your own words. For example, you might claim that the novel shows the divide between the groups is more about circumstance than character, and then describe a moment where the two sides behave in a way that looks more alike than different.

Your reply (two or three sentences, to one classmate)

Read one classmate's claim. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add a second example from the novel that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, using the novel.

Posting rules
 
›Post your own claim first, before you can see classmates' posts.
›Use at least one specific event from the novel, described in your own words.
›Be respectful in disagreement. Argue with the idea, not the person.
